sweep_summary: Menominee (meno1252, catalog: weight-hedged; deciding source Bloomfield 1962:19-20 as carried by StressTyp2, supported by Cudworth 2019's summary of Milligan 2005). the list of works with stress in the title holds one item, Milligan 2005 'Menominee prosodic structure' (UW-Madison PhD, vi+167 pp.), which is squarely about Menominee word stress (the only instrumental study: pitch = main correlate of primary stress, duration of secondary; heavy syllables stressed; multiple primary stresses; final syllables unstressed, per Cudworth 2019:25, 43, 46). It is still not readable: HathiTrust has a search-only digitisation (wu.89095481388, in copyright; the site could not be reached by automated download to non-browser clients), UW-Madison holds print (Verona Shelving Facility, AWB M6546 M375) plus a ProQuest/UMI copy behind login; MINDS@UW, archive.org, OpenLibrary, PAC OJS, the author's Macalester page have nothing; Priority to acquire: high (it would settle the hedge first-hand). Newly downloaded and read: Bloomfield 1928 Menomini Texts (archive.org, public-domain mark; saved), whose pp. XIII-XIV mark three stress/pitch degrees and say the accents are 'not distinctive of word-meaning', with no placement rule (silent). Re-read from the page scan: Bever 1967 p.36, an open MIT dissertation restating Bloomfield 1962's rules (primary stress on every long vowel in the penult or before a short-vowel syllable; secondary on even syllables; finals never stressed; phrase domain), which confirms the catalog's classification but does not supersede Bloomfield 1962. Bloomfield 1962 itself remains controlled-lending only on archive.org (search-inside returns 'Item not available'). written and appended in Net: nothing read contradicts the catalog; the hedge stays until Milligan 2005 ch. 4-5 or Bloomfield 1962 pp. 19-20 is read first-hand.

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive (long vowel = heavy), non-culminative: every long vowel that is penultimate or followed by a short-vowel syllable gets primary stress, so a word may carry several primary stresses and a word with no long vowel has no primary stress; secondary stress is an even-syllable (iambic) count; final syllables never stressed; the domain is the phrase/compound. This matches the catalog's weight-hedged coding and the StressTyp2-carried Bloomfield passage word for word in content. It is a first-hand reading of a secondary restatement, not of Bloomfield's own paragraph, and the file was already downloaded in the 2026-09-16 check; the only file newly downloaded in this search of works with stress in the title (Bloomfield 1928, pp. XIII-XIV) only says the accents are 'not distinctive of word-meaning' and gives no placement rule.

sources.quote: p.36: "Until these rules apply all vowels are unstressed. Primary stress rules apply only to long vowels in certain positions: 10) V̄ → primary stress a) —C₁²VC₂²# (i.e. in next to last syllable) b) —C₁²V̆ (i.e. preceding a syllable with a short vowel). These rules apply to any syntactic unit, not just to words. Thus, although final syllables cannot receive either primary or secondary stress ..."
sources.note: A formal restatement of Bloomfield 1962's stress rules (cited there as M 1.51): every long vowel in the penult, or before a short-vowel syllable, takes primary stress (so several primary stresses per word are possible); secondary stress on even-numbered syllables, never on a constituent-final syllable; the domain is the syntactic unit (compound/phrase), not only the word.
